seoDescription: Learn the fundamentals of Django views and URL routing in this beginner-friendly tutorial. Discover how Django processes user requests by mapping URLs to specific views using URL patterns and regular expressions. This guide walks you through setting up app-specific `urls.py` files to keep your project organized, avoiding clutter in your main URL configuration.

chapters.title: Introduction to Django's Default URLs
chapters.description: This chapter introduces the default homepage and admin section of a new Django project and questions how Django knows where to route these requests.

chapters.title: The Core of Django Routing: `urls.py`
chapters.description: Learn how Django's main `urls.py` file uses URL patterns and regular expressions to match user requests and determine the appropriate response.

chapters.title: Mapping URLs to Responses
chapters.description: This section explains how, upon finding a matching URL pattern, Django uses the second part of the mapping to determine how to respond to the request.

chapters.title: Scaling Problem: A Cluttered `urls.py`
chapters.description: Discover why adding all of an application's URL patterns directly into the main project's `urls.py` file is a poor design choice that leads to clutter.

chapters.title: Best Practice: App-Specific URL Files
chapters.description: Learn the proper way to structure a large Django project by keeping each app's URLs contained within its own `urls.py` file.

chapters.title: Creating an App's `urls.py` and View
chapters.description: Follow a step-by-step guide to create a new `urls.py` file inside an app, import the necessary views, and define the app's first URL pattern.

chapters.title: Including App URLs in the Main Project
chapters.description: Learn to use the `include()` function in your main project's `urls.py` to delegate routing for a specific path to your app's URL configuration.

chapters.title: Creating the View Function
chapters.description: This chapter guides you through writing a basic view function in `views.py` that takes a request and returns a simple `HttpResponse`.

chapters.title: Reviewing the Full Request-Response Cycle
chapters.description: A final, cohesive walkthrough of how a user request flows from the browser, through the project and app URL files, to the view, and back as a response.

summary:
## Django's Request-Response Cycle When a user requests a URL from a Django site, the following process occurs: 1. Django receives the request. 2. It looks at the main project's `urls.py` file to find a matching URL pattern. 3. Once a pattern is matched, it calls the associated **view** function or includes another URL configuration. 4. The view function processes the request and returns an **`HttpResponse`**. 5. Django sends this response back to the user's browser. ## URL Routing with `urls.py` The core of Django's routing system is the `urlpatterns` list found in `urls.py` files. Each item in the list maps a URL pattern to a handler. - **URL Patterns**: These are regular expressions that match against the requested URL path. - `r'^music/'`: Matches any URL that starts with `music/`. - `r'^$'`: Matches an empty path, typically the index or homepage of a section. - **Handlers**: The action to take when a pattern matches. This can be a view function or, for better organization, an `include()` to another `urls.py` file. > [!TIP] > A caret (`^`) in a regular expression marks the beginning of the string, and a dollar sign (`$`) marks the end. `r'^music/$'` would match `/music/` exactly, but not `/music/details/`. ## Best Practice: App-Specific URLs For any project with more than a few pages, it's crucial to keep it organized. Instead of putting all URL patterns in the main project's `urls.py`, each app should manage its own URLs. 1. **Create an `app/urls.py` file**: Inside your app's directory (e.g., `music/`), create a new `urls.py` file to hold patterns specific to that app. 2. **Use `include()`**: In the main project's `urls.py`, use the `include()` function to delegate all URLs under a certain path to the app's `urls.py` file. > [!IMPORTANT] > This design keeps apps modular and self-contained. If you want to reuse the `music` app in another project, you can bring its URLs along with it easily. ## Creating a View A **view** is a Python function that handles a web request and returns a web response. - It must accept at least one argument, typically named **`request`**, which is an `HttpRequest` object containing information about the request. - It must return an **`HttpResponse`** object (or a subclass). This object contains the content that will be sent back to the browser. - A simple view can return plain text or HTML directly inside the `HttpResponse`. ## Code Examples **Main Project `website/urls.py`:** ```python from django.conf.urls import url, include from django.contrib import admin urlpatterns = [ url(r'^admin/', admin.site.urls), # Any request to /music/... is handled by the music app's urls.py url(r'^music/', include('music.urls')), ] ``` **App `music/urls.py`:** ```python from django.conf.urls import url from . import views urlpatterns = [ # /music/ -> calls the index view url(r'^$', views.index, name='index'), ] ``` **App `music/views.py`:** ```python from django.http import HttpResponse def index(request): return HttpResponse("

This is the music app homepage

") ```
